gloss: tend, shepherd, graze; keep company; friend, neighbour; pasture; thought, desire
summary: The verb is to tend a flock and lead it to pasture, and of the flock to graze; its participle רֹעֶה is the shepherd, from Abel (Gen 4:2) to Yahweh himself (Gen 48:15; Psa 23:1), and so a people’s ruler, whom Yahweh tells to “shepherd my people Israel” (2Sa 5:2). The same letters give רֵעַ, the friend or neighbour, the other man one lives beside, whom Israel is to “love as yourself” (Lev 19:18), and the verb “keep company with” (Pro 13:20); מִרְעֶה and מַרְעִית are the pasture and the flock pastured, “the sheep of his pasture” (Psa 100:3). A smaller group, רֵעַ “thought”, רְעוּת and רַעְיוֹן “striving”, and Daniel’s Aramaic רַעְיוֹן “thoughts”, have the same consonants, though how they join the rest is not shown; Arabic raʿā “pasture; tend; rule; be mindful of”, Akkadian reʾû “shepherd” and rūʾu “friend”, and Ugaritic rʿ “friend” all keep the same ʿ.

words.gloss: tend, shepherd; graze, feed on; keep company with
words.summary: About 174 uses, nearly all qal, and more than half of them the participle רֹעֶה, “shepherd”. The flock’s keeper leads it to grass and water and guards it; the beasts graze; and a king or prophet “shepherds” the people. A few uses, with the same letters, mean to keep company with someone: the verb of רֵעַ, “friend”.

stems.gloss: tend, shepherd; graze; keep company with

senses.definition: To keep a flock: lead it to pasture and water, gather and carry the weak, and defend it from beasts. The participle is the shepherd or herdsman.

evidence.note: “Abel was a רֹעֵה צֹאן, and Cain a worker of the ground.”
“Like a רֹעֶה he will shepherd (יִרְעֶה) his flock; he will gather the lambs in his arm, carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.”
“Should not the shepherds shepherd (יִרְעוּ) the flock?” The next verses say what that is.
What the shepherds did not do: strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind the broken, bring back the strayed, seek the lost.
David: “Your servant was רֹעֶה for his father among the flock, and a lion came … and I went out after it and struck it and delivered it from its mouth.”
“As the רֹעֶה delivers from the lion’s mouth two legs or a piece of an ear.”
“Water the sheep, and go, shepherd them (רְעוּ)”; Rachel came with her father’s sheep, “for she was רֹעָה”.
Joseph, seventeen, “was shepherding the flock with his brothers”.
Strife between “the herdsmen (רֹעֵי) of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s”.
“The men are רֹעֵי צֹאן … every רֹעֵה צֹאן is an abomination to Egypt.”
“Moses was shepherding the flock of Jethro his father-in-law.”
The shepherds drive off Reuel’s daughters; Moses delivers them and waters the flock.
The youngest “is shepherding the sheep”: David.
Doeg the Edomite, “chief of the shepherds who were Saul’s”.
In the land made desolate there will again be a habitation of רֹעִים resting their flocks.
“My dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd’s tent.”

senses.gloss: shepherd a people: lead, rule and care for
senses.definition: To lead and keep a people as a shepherd keeps a flock: said of Yahweh, of the king he appoints, and of Israel’s rulers, priests and prophets, who answer to him for the flock. Its parallels are “be prince over”, “lead out and bring in”, and “lead”.

evidence.note: “Yahweh said to you, You shall shepherd (תִרְעֶה) my people Israel, and you shall be נָגִיד over Israel”: shepherding set beside ruling.
He took David from the sheepfolds, from following the ewes, “to shepherd Jacob his people … and he shepherded them according to the integrity of his heart, and led them by the skill of his hands”.
Moses asks for a man “who will go out before them and come in before them … that the congregation of Yahweh be not as sheep that have no רֹעֶה”: Joshua.
“I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains as sheep that have no רֹעֶה”: their king about to fall.
Jacob: “the God who has shepherded me (הָרֹעֶה אֹתִי) all my life to this day”.
“From the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, from there is the רֹעֶה, the stone of Israel.”
“Yahweh is my shepherd (רֹעִי); I shall not lack.” Grass, still waters, paths of righteousness, the rod and staff follow (Psa 23:2–4).
“Give ear, רֹעֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל, you who lead Joseph like a flock.”
“Save your people and bless your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them for ever.”
“Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock?”: Moses and Aaron (Psa 77:21).
“I will give you shepherds according to my heart, who will shepherd you with knowledge and understanding.”
“Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture … I will set up shepherds over them who will shepherd them, and they shall fear no more.”
“The shepherds transgressed against me”, set beside the priests, the handlers of the law and the prophets.
“I am against the shepherds … they shall no longer shepherd themselves.”
“I myself will shepherd my sheep, and I will make them lie down.”
“I will raise up over them one רֹעֶה, and he shall shepherd them, my servant David; he shall shepherd them and be their רֹעֶה.”
“My servant David shall be king over them, and they shall all have one רֹעֶה.”
The ruler from Bethlehem (Mic 5:1) “shall stand and shepherd in the strength of Yahweh … for now he shall be great to the ends of the earth”.
“Shepherd your people with your rod, the flock of your inheritance.”
Yahweh “says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and he shall perform all my pleasure”.
The prophet told to “shepherd the flock of slaughter”, who gives it up: “I will not shepherd you.”
“Woe to the worthless shepherd who forsakes the flock!”
“Sword, awake against my shepherd, against the man who is my fellow … strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.”
The words of the wise “are given from one shepherd”.
Jeremiah: “I have not hastened from being a shepherd after you.”

senses.definition: Of animals, to graze, or to graze a place bare; and, by a figure, to feed on something, to take it in as one’s food, or to eat up and lay waste.

evidence.note: Seven cows came up out of the Nile “and they grazed (וַתִּרְעֶינָה) in the reed-grass”.
“Let neither flocks nor herds graze in front of that mountain.”
“The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together.”
“The wolf and the lamb shall graze as one.”
“In that day your cattle will graze in wide pastures.”
“The oxen were ploughing and the donkeys grazing beside them.”
“Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything; let them not graze nor drink water.”
“My beloved is mine and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.”
The remnant of Israel “shall graze and lie down, and none shall make them afraid”.
“Ephraim feeds on wind (רֹעֶה רוּחַ) and pursues the east wind”: his treaties with Assyria and Egypt.
The idol-maker “feeds on ashes; a deceived heart has turned him aside”.
“The heart of the discerning seeks knowledge, but the mouth of fools feeds on folly.”
“The lips of the righteous feed many.”
“Trust in Yahweh and do good; dwell in the land and feed on faithfulness (וּרְעֵה אֱמוּנָה).” Could also be read “befriend faithfulness”.
“Like sheep they are laid in the grave; death shall shepherd them (מָוֶת יִרְעֵם).”
“The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds”: drive them off.
The men of Noph and Tahpanhes “have grazed the crown of your head”.
“They shall shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword.”
The wicked “feeds on the barren that does not bear”.

senses.gloss: keep company with, be a companion of
senses.definition: To associate with someone, to be his companion: the verb of רֵעַ, “friend”. In Proverbs the participle with a plural object names the company a man keeps.

evidence.note: “He who walks with (הוֹלֵךְ אֶת) the wise will be wise, but the companion of fools (רֹעֶה כְסִילִים) will be broken (יֵרוֹעַ)”: the parallel fixes the sense, with a play on רעע.
“He who keeps the law is a wise son, but the companion of gluttons shames his father.”
“He who loves wisdom gladdens his father, but the companion of harlots squanders wealth.”

stems.gloss: make a companion, attend as friend

senses.definition: To take or serve someone as companion; once, of the companion who attended Samson at his wedding.

evidence.note: “Samson’s wife was given to his companion (לְמֵרֵעֵהוּ), whom he had made his companion (אֲשֶׁר רֵעָה לוֹ)”, one of the thirty companions of Jdg 14:11.

senses.definition: To make oneself someone’s friend; once, in a warning.

evidence.note: “Do not make friends (אַל־תִּתְרַע) with a man given to anger, and with a man of wrath do not go, lest you learn his ways”: the parallel “go with” fixes it.
תִרְעֶה → ποιμανεῖς; also PSA 23:1 word 4 and EZK 34:23 word 5.
Mic 5:1 joined to 2Sa 5:2: from Bethlehem “shall come a ruler who will shepherd (ποιμανεῖ) my people Israel”.
“Shepherd my sheep.”
The elders of Ephesus are to “shepherd the ecclesia of God, which he purchased with his own blood”.
“Shepherd the flock of God among you.”
“The Lamb in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to springs of living water”, in the words of Isa 49:9–10.
“He will shepherd them with a rod of iron”, Psa 2:9 in the Greek, which reads the consonants of תְּרֹעֵם “you will break them” as from this root.
רֹעֵה → ποιμὴν; also NUM 27:17 word 19, EZK 34:23 word 3, ZEC 13:7 word 13.
“I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
“There shall be one flock, one shepherd”: Ezk 34:23; 37:24.
Zec 13:7 quoted: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.”
The crowds were “like sheep having no shepherd”: Num 27:17; 1Ki 22:17.
“The God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep”, in the words of Isa 63:11.
“You were like sheep going astray, but have now returned to the shepherd and overseer of your souls.”
“When the chief shepherd appears.”
יִרְעוּ → βόσκω; also GEN 37:12 word 3, ISA 11:7 word 3.
“Feed my lambs.”
“Feed my sheep.”

parallels.note: “Prince”: shepherding the people is ruling them.

phrases.gloss: as sheep that have no shepherd
feeding on wind: chasing what gives nothing

words.summary: About 190 uses. The man one lives and deals with: a close friend, a fellow, the neighbour whose goods and wife and good name the law guards, and, with אִישׁ, simply “the other”, as English says “one another”.

senses.definition: A friend or close companion, chosen and trusted; set beside brother, and once beside the wife of one’s bosom.

evidence.note: “Your brother, your son or daughter, the wife of your bosom, or your רֵעַ who is as your own soul”, who might entice you to other gods.
“Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his רֵעַ.”
“A רֵעַ loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
“A man of many רֵעִים comes to ruin, but there is one who loves and sticks closer than a brother.”
“Do not forsake your friend and your father’s friend.”
“As for a friend, as for a brother to me, I went about mourning.”
“When Job’s three רֵעִים heard of all this evil.”
Yahweh’s anger against Eliphaz “and your two friends”; Job prays “for his friends”.
“He and Hirah his friend the Adullamite.”
“Amnon had a friend, Jonadab.”
“Ahithophel was the king’s counsellor, and Hushai the Archite was רֵעַ הַמֶּלֶךְ”: a title at court.
“Do not trust in a friend; put no confidence in a companion.”
“You have put lover and friend far from me.”
“This is my beloved, and this is my friend.”

senses.definition: The other man beside whom one lives, whose life, goods, landmark, wife and good name the law protects: the fellow Israelite, one of “the sons of your people”.

evidence.note: “You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your people, but you shall love your רֵעַ as yourself.”
“You shall not bear false witness against your רֵעַ; you shall not covet your רֵעַ’s house … his wife … or anything that is your רֵעַ’s.”
“You shall not oppress your neighbour or rob him.”
“You shall not stand against the blood of your neighbour.”
If a man schemes against his neighbour to kill him.
Goods kept for a neighbour.
The manslayer who kills his neighbour unawares.
“You shall not move your neighbour’s landmark.”
The betrothed girl is already “his neighbour’s wife”.
“Kill each man his brother, each man his רֵעַ, each man his near kinsman”: the three in a row.
“Do not say to your neighbour, Go and come again … Do not devise evil against your neighbour, who dwells securely beside you.”
He “does no evil to his רֵעַ, nor takes up a reproach against his near one”.
“Speak truth each man with his neighbour.”
“They shall no longer teach each man his neighbour, saying, Know Yahweh.”
Yahweh has given the kingdom “to your neighbour, who is better than you”.

senses.definition: With אִישׁ “each man”, the other of a pair or group: “each … his fellow”, one another; of things as well as people.

evidence.note: “They said each man to his רֵעַ, Come, let us make bricks.”
Abram “laid each half over against its רֵעַ”: of the pieces of the covenant animals.
“They said each man to his fellow, Come, let us cast lots.”
Yahweh set every man’s sword against his fellow.
“They asked each other of their welfare.”
“Those who feared Yahweh spoke with one another.”

senses.definition: A woman’s lover, in figures of Israel’s unfaithfulness; once the husband himself.

evidence.note: “You have played the harlot with many רֵעִים; yet return to me.”
“As a wife treacherously departs from her רֵעַ, so have you dealt treacherously with me.”
“A woman loved by a רֵעַ and an adulteress.”
“All her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.”
לְרֵעֲךָ → πλησίον; πλησίον renders רֵעַ about twenty times.
Lev 19:18 quoted: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself”, the second commandment.
“And who is my neighbour?”
“Which of these was neighbour to him?” “The one who showed mercy on him.”
The commandments summed up in Lev 19:18; “love works no ill to a neighbour”.
“The royal law.”
Zec 8:16: “speak truth each man with his neighbour.”
Jer 31:34 quoted.
רֵעֲךָ → φίλον; also JOB 2:11 word 3.
“Greater love has no one than this, that one lay down his life for his friends … I have called you friends.”
רֵעַ → ἑταῖρος.
To Judas: “Companion, why have you come?”

parallels.note: “Brother”, beside it in law and proverb.
“The sons of your people”, the parallel that fixes the neighbour of Lev 19:18 as the fellow Israelite.

phrases.gloss: each to his fellow: to one another
you shall love your neighbour as yourself
the king’s friend: a court title

senses.definition: Grass or ground where flocks and herds graze; the want of it drives herdsmen to move.

evidence.note: “We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no מִרְעֶה for your servants’ flocks, for the famine is heavy in Canaan.”
“To seek מִרְעֶה for their flocks; and they found rich and good מִרְעֶה.”
“I will shepherd them in good pasture.”
“Is it too little for you to graze the good pasture, that you must tread down the rest of your pastures with your feet?”
“The herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture.”
Her princes “like deer that find no pasture”.
The city becomes “a pasture of flocks”.
The wild donkey ranges the mountains as its pasture.
Nineveh, the lions’ den and “the feeding place of the young lions”.
מִרְעֶה → νομὴ.
“If anyone enters by me he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture.”

words.summary: A companion or close friend, at times one attached to a great man or a bridegroom. Several tokens filed under it are רֵעַ with the preposition מִן (“from his fellow”), so its own uses are about half the count.

senses.definition: A companion attached to someone: a king’s confidant, a bridegroom’s attendants, a man’s friends.

evidence.note: “Abimelech came from Gerar with Ahuzzath his מֵרֵעַ and Phicol the commander of his army.”
“They took thirty מֵרֵעִים, and they were with him”: the bridegroom’s companions.
“I gave her to your companion.”
Abner: “I show kindness to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers and to his friends.”
“All the brothers of the poor hate him; how much more do his friends go far from him!”
לְמֵרֵעֵהוּ → φίλων; also JDG 15:2 word 9.
“The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly”: the bridegroom’s companion of Jdg 14:11, 20.

senses.definition: The pasturing, and so the flock under a shepherd’s keeping. In “the sheep of his pasture” it is Israel as Yahweh’s own flock.

evidence.note: “He made us, and we are his, his people and צֹאן מַרְעִיתוֹ.”
“We are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand.”
“You are my sheep, the sheep of my pasture; you are men, and I am your God.”
“Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture.”
“The shepherds have become brutish … and all their מַרְעִית is scattered”: the flock itself.
“Yahweh is laying waste their pasture.”
“On all bare heights shall be their pasture.”
“According to their pasture they were filled; they were filled, and their heart was lifted up; therefore they forgot me.”
מַרְעִיתִי → ποιμνίου.
“Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.”

words.summary: Only in the Song of Songs, always “my רַעְיָה”, the bridegroom’s word for the bride.

senses.definition: The bridegroom’s name for the bride: his companion, set beside “my sister, my dove, my beautiful one”.

evidence.note: “Open to me, my sister, my רַעְיָה, my dove, my perfect one.”
“Arise, my רַעְיָה, my beautiful one, and come away.”
“Like a lily among thorns, so is my רַעְיָה among the daughters.”
“You are altogether beautiful, my רַעְיָה; there is no blemish in you.”

words.summary: Only in Ecclesiastes, in “רְעוּת רוּחַ”: what a man reaches after, which turns out to be wind. Ezra’s Aramaic רְעוּת “will, pleasure” (Ezr 5:17; 7:18), which answers to Hebrew רָצָה “be pleased” (see the ratson entry), supports “desire, striving”, and if so the word belongs with that root; Hosea’s “Ephraim feeds on wind” (Hos 12:2) suggests “feeding on wind” from the verb. Which the Preacher meant the text does not settle.

senses.definition: A reaching after, a desire: in the Preacher’s verdict on man’s work under the sun, the pursuit of what cannot be held.

evidence.note: “I saw all the works done under the sun, and behold, all is vapour and רְעוּת רוּחַ.”
All toil and skill “is a man’s rivalry with his neighbour (מֵרֵעֵהוּ); this too is vapour and רְעוּת רוּחַ”.
“Better a handful with quiet than two handfuls with toil and רְעוּת רוּחַ.”
“Better the sight of the eyes than the wandering of desire (נָפֶשׁ); this too is vapour and רְעוּת רוּחַ.”

words.summary: The feminine of רֵעַ, used as it is with אִישׁ: “each woman … her neighbour”, and of animals, “each with her mate”.

senses.definition: Another woman, a woman’s neighbour; and, of birds, each one’s mate.

evidence.note: “Let every man ask of his neighbour (רֵעֵהוּ) and every woman of her neighbour (רְעוּתָהּ).”
“Teach your daughters a lament, and each woman her neighbour a dirge.”
“Let the king give her royal place to her רְעוּת who is better than she.”
“Let those that are left eat each one the flesh of her fellow.”
The birds of prey gathered “each with her mate … none shall lack her mate”.

words.summary: Twice, in Psalm 139, a man’s thought and God’s thoughts. It has the same letters as רֵעַ “friend”; Jewish Aramaic רַעְיוֹנָא “thought” and scripture’s own Aramaic רַעְיוֹן (Dan 2:30) give its sense. How it is tied to the root’s “tend, graze” is not shown; Arabic raʿā “be mindful of, regard” is a possible bridge.

senses.definition: What is in a man’s mind, known to God before it is spoken; and God’s own purposes.

evidence.note: “You know my sitting down and my rising up; you understand my thought (לְרֵעִי) from afar.”
“How precious to me are your thoughts (רֵעֶיךָ), God! How great is their sum!”
לְרֵעִי → διαλογισμούς.
“That the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

words.gloss: friend (of the king), a court title
words.summary: A form of רֵעַ used for the king’s friend, an office held by Hushai under David and by Zabud under Solomon.

senses.definition: A title at the king’s court: his trusted companion and adviser.

evidence.note: “Hushai, David’s רֵעֶה, came into the city.”
Among Solomon’s officers: “Zabud son of Nathan, priest, the king’s רֵעֶה”.
רֵעֶה → ἑταῖρος; also 2SA 16:16 word 6.

words.summary: Three times in Ecclesiastes, beside רְעוּת: the striving of the heart. The same word in scripture’s Aramaic is a man’s thoughts (Dan 2:30).

senses.definition: The heart’s reaching after a thing, set beside toil.

evidence.note: “What has a man from all his toil and from the רַעְיוֹן of his heart, with which he toils under the sun?”
To know wisdom and madness: “this too is רַעְיוֹן רוּחַ”.

senses.definition: The young women who go with a girl: her companions.

evidence.note: Jephthah’s daughter “went, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains”.
“The virgins after her, her companions, are brought to you.”

words.summary: Once, of cattle raised at grass, as against stall-fattened ones.

senses.definition: Pasture, in “cattle of pasture”: beasts grazed in the open, set against fattened ones.

evidence.note: Solomon’s daily provision: “ten fat oxen (בָקָר בְּרִאִים), and twenty oxen of pasture (בָּקָר רְעִי), and a hundred sheep”.

words.summary: In Daniel’s Aramaic, the thoughts of a man’s heart, which alarm the king and which God reveals.

senses.definition: What passes through the mind, “the thoughts of your heart”; troubling thoughts in a crisis.

evidence.note: “As for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what would be after this.”
“That you may know the thoughts of your heart (רַעְיוֹנֵי לִבְבָךְ).”
Daniel was appalled for a moment, “and his thoughts alarmed him”.
The king’s colour changed “and his thoughts alarmed him”.
“My thoughts greatly alarmed me.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܪܥܝܐ (rāʿyā), for ποιμήν: the shepherd, and Jesus as the good shepherd.

senses.definition: A keeper of sheep; Jesus the shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, and those who keep his flock.

evidence.note: “I am the good ܪܥܝܐ; the good ܪܥܝܐ lays down his life for the sheep.”
“One flock, one shepherd.”
Zec 13:7: “I will strike the shepherd.”
Shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s verb ܪܥܐ (rʿā), for ποιμαίνω and βόσκω.

senses.gloss: feed, tend (a flock); shepherd a people
senses.definition: To feed and keep sheep or swine, and to shepherd God’s people.

evidence.note: “Feed my lambs … feed my sheep.”
Mic 5:1 with 2Sa 5:2: a ruler “who will shepherd my people Israel”.
Sent into the fields to feed swine.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܡܪܥܝܬܐ (marʿītā), for ποίμνιον and ποίμνη: the same word as Hebrew מַרְעִית.

senses.definition: A flock, and the ecclesia as God’s flock.

evidence.note: “Take heed to yourselves and to all the ܡܪܥܝܬܐ.”
“Who shepherds a flock and does not eat of its milk?”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܪܥܝܐ “pasture”, once, for νομή.

senses.definition: Pasture found by the sheep that enter by the door.

evidence.note: “He will go in and go out and find ܪܥܝܐ.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܪܥܝܢܐ (reʿyānā), common for νοῦς and διάνοια: the same word as Daniel’s Aramaic רַעְיוֹן.

senses.definition: The mind, the seat of thought and understanding, which is to be renewed.

evidence.note: “Be transformed by the renewing of your ܪܥܝܢܐ.”
“With my ܪܥܝܢܐ I serve the law of God.”
“We have the mind of Christ.”
Deu 6:5: “with all your mind”.
“He opened their mind to understand the scriptures.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܐܬܪܥܝ (ethpaal of ܪܥܐ), for φρονέω, ἐνθυμέομαι and διαλογίζομαι.

stems.gloss: think, ponder, set the mind on

senses.gloss: think, ponder; set one’s mind on
senses.definition: To turn a thing over in the mind, and to set one’s mind on it.

evidence.note: “While he thought on these things.”
“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus.”
“Set your mind on things above.”
“They reasoned among themselves.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܬܪܥܝܬܐ (tarʿītā), for φρόνημα and διάνοια: the mind and its purposes.

senses.definition: The mind as set on something, and its thoughts and purposes.

evidence.note: “The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the spirit is life and peace.”
“He has scattered the proud in the thought of their hearts.”
The word of God “discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart”.

cognates.gloss: (of cattle) pasture; tend, pasture (cattle); keep, guard; rule, govern; rāʿin shepherd, ruler; raʿiyya flock, subjects; marʿan pasture
cognates.note: The same range as the Hebrew verb: cattle grazing, the herdsman keeping them, and the ruler “keeping” his people, who are his raʿiyya, his flock. Its noun marʿan is Hebrew מִרְעֶה letter for letter.

evidence.note: “The cattle pastured”; رَعْىٌ “The keeping, or tending, animals; pasturing, or feeding, them; and defending them from the enemy … And hence … managing or ruling or governing”; رَعَى الأَمِيرُ رَعِيَّتَهُ “The prince ruled, or governed, his subjects”.
“A keeper, or guarder, or pastor, of cattle … A ruler, or governor … who manages … the affairs of a people.”
“Cattle kept, tended, or pastured”; the plural “for the subjects”.
“A pasturage, or place of pasture.”

cognates.gloss: be mindful, regardful of (an affair); observe
cognates.note: The same Arabic verb used of keeping a thing in mind; a possible bridge from “tend” to Hebrew רֵעַ “thought”, but not shown.

evidence.note: “رَعَى أَمْرَهُ … He was mindful, or regardful, of his affair, or case”; in the Kur’an “they did not observe it with its right, or due, observance”.

cognates.gloss: pasture, graze, shepherd (verb); rēʾû shepherd, herdsman
cognates.note: Akkadian rēʾû “shepherd” is among the commonest words of the language, used of kings as shepherds of their people as well as of herdsmen.

evidence.note: “pasture; graze; shepherd; tend.”
“herdsman; shepherd” (×1612).
“herbage?; pasture”; forms rîtu, riʾītu.

cognates.note: Akkadian keeps the friend apart from the shepherd (rūʾu beside rēʾû), as Hebrew רֵעַ stands beside רֹעֶה.

evidence.note: “colleague; companion; friend.”

cognates.note: Ugaritic writes ʿ and ġ with different letters; rʿ has ʿ, the same sound as Arabic raʿā “pasture”, so the friend and the shepherd show no split behind ע.

evidence.note: “friend” (H. rēaʿ and rēʿeh; Imperial Aramaic rʿ; Akkadian ruʾu). Read from the scan’s text layer, which is garbled here.
“[Heb. roʿe] n.m. SHEPHERD. KAI 37 B 8 (Ph) lrʿm … ‘<Paid out> for the <ransom of the> shepherds who were seized by Paphos’.”

cognates.gloss: graze; rʿy shepherd, herdsman; rʿyn care, protection

evidence.note: Verb “GRAZE” (J745/10); rʿy “SHEPHERD, HERDSMAN” (G1142/7); rʿyn “CARE, PROTECTION”; rʿt “FLOCK, HERD (?)”. Read from the scan’s text layer.

cognates.note: The Targums use it where the Hebrew has רָעָה (Targ. Gen 30:31; Exo 34:3; Isa 40:11).

evidence.note: “to feed; to graze. Targ. Gen. XXX, 31; 36. Targ. Ex. XXXIV, 3.”
“shepherd. Targ. Is. XL, 11. Targ. II Sam. XXIV, 17.”

cognates.note: The Targum of Psalms has רַעְיוֹנִין where the Hebrew has מַחֲשָׁבוֹת “thoughts” (Targ. Psa 40:6 Ms.): the same word as Daniel’s Aramaic רַעְיוֹן.

evidence.note: “desire, thought. Targ. Ps. XXXII, 11 … Pl. רַעְיוֹנִין … Targ. Ps. XL, 6 Ms. (ed. רעותך; h. text מחשבת׳).”

doctrine.statement: Yahweh is Israel’s shepherd: Jacob speaks of “the God who has shepherded me all my life” (Gen 48:15), and David, “Yahweh is my shepherd; I shall not lack” (Psa 23:1). He made David shepherd of his people, “you shall shepherd my people Israel and be prince over Israel” (2Sa 5:2; Psa 78:70–72). When Israel’s shepherds fed themselves and scattered the flock, Yahweh said, “I myself will shepherd my sheep” (Ezk 34:2–15), and in the same breath, “I will raise up over them one shepherd, my servant David; he shall shepherd them” (Ezk 34:23), who will be king over Israel gathered from the nations into their own land, “and they shall all have one shepherd … and David my servant shall be their prince for ever” (Ezk 37:21–25). Micah’s ruler from Bethlehem “shall stand and shepherd in the strength of Yahweh” and be great to the ends of the earth (Mic 5:1–3). Matthew says that ruler is Jesus, born in Bethlehem, “who will shepherd my people Israel” (Mat 2:6). Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep … there shall be one flock, one shepherd” (Jhn 10:11, 16). Zechariah’s “strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zec 13:7) he applies to his arrest (Mat 26:31). God “brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep” (Heb 13:20), and Peter tells the elders that “when the chief shepherd appears” they will receive a crown (1Pe 5:4). From the verses: Yahweh shepherds his flock through the son of David he raised up; the shepherd was struck and raised, and the reign Ezekiel describes, one king over a regathered Israel in its land, is still to come, at his appearing.

Those set over God’s people are called shepherds and answer to him for the flock. Through Ezekiel Yahweh charges Israel’s shepherds that they fed themselves and not the sheep: they did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the broken, bring back the strayed or seek the lost, but ruled them with force, so the flock was scattered; “I will require my sheep at their hand” (Ezk 34:2–10). Jeremiah: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture”, and the promise of “shepherds according to my heart, who will shepherd you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 23:1–4; 3:15). Jesus sets the good shepherd who lays down his life against the hired man who flees (Jhn 10:11–13), and tells Peter, “feed my lambs … shepherd my sheep” (Jhn 21:15–17). Paul tells the elders of Ephesus to “shepherd the ecclesia of God, which he purchased with his own blood”, against wolves that would not spare the flock (Act 20:28–29), and Peter, to shepherd the flock willingly, “not as lording it over” them, but as examples (1Pe 5:2–3). From the verses: to shepherd God’s people is to feed and care for them for his sake, not to rule them for one’s own, and he holds the shepherds to account.

The law forbids wronging one’s רֵעַ: false witness against him, coveting his house or wife, robbing him, standing against his blood (Exo 20:16–17; Lev 19:13, 16), and sums it up: “you shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your people, but you shall love your רֵעַ as yourself; I am Yahweh” (Lev 19:18). In the same chapter the stranger who lives among Israel is to be loved “as yourself” as well (Lev 19:34). Jesus calls Lev 19:18 the second commandment, like the first, and says the law and the prophets hang on the two (Mat 22:37–40). Asked “who is my neighbour?”, he answers with the Samaritan who showed mercy to a wounded Jew, and asks which of the three “was neighbour” to him: “the one who showed mercy” (Luk 10:29–37). Paul: every commandment “is summed up in this word, you shall love your neighbour as yourself; love works no ill to a neighbour; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law” (Rom 13:9–10; Gal 5:14), and James calls it “the royal law” (Jas 2:8). From the verses: the neighbour of the law is first the fellow Israelite, but Jesus turns the question from whom one must love to whom one will show mercy, and so makes the neighbour whoever is in need.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Numbers 10 (רְעוּאֵל, Num 10:29). The corpus keys the root רעה. BDB splits it into three roots (t.dk.* “pasture”, t.dl.* “associate, friend”, t.dm.* “desire, thought”); this entry keeps them as one spelling, and the cognates for the shepherd and friend words (Arabic raʿā, Ugaritic rʿ, Sabaic rʿy) show ʿ throughout, with no split behind ע. The verb’s three BDB keys t.dk.aa, t.dl.aa and t.dl.ad count the same 189 tokens (the verb’s 174 plus Reu and four רָעָה “evil” tokens filed by spelling), so the verb names t.dk.aa only; t.dl.aa and t.dl.ad are left unclaimed. DATABASE FAULT: the word_info rows for about 163 of the verb’s tokens carry root בית (from the place name בֵּית עֵקֶד הָרֹעִים, b.bp.bn, 2Ki 10:12), so lexicon-brief lists them as another root’s verb and lexicon-support counts the verb at 21 uses; the senses here were written from the full list of tokens. Overlaps: t.dl.ab (רֵעַ friend) and t.dm.ab (רֵעַ thought) share four surfaces (Psa 139:17; Pro 6:3; Job 35:4; 42:7); only Psa 139:2, 17 are “thought”. t.dl.al (מֵרֵעַ) shares eight surfaces with רֵעַ plus מִן (Gen 31:49; Jer 9:3; Pro 12:26; Job 6:14; Ecc 4:4 etc.), which are not this noun. Ezra’s Aramaic רְעוּת “will” (xt.al.ab, Ezr 5:17; 7:18) and the Peshitta’s ܪܥܐ “reconcile” and ܬܪܥܘܬܐ “reconciliation” (SEDRA root 1775) are in ratson.json under רצה, where Aramaic ע answers to the older ṣ́ (Arabic raḍiya); the Phoenician rʿt “resolution” (Krahmalkov p. 445, KAI 60) is a lead for that entry, not cited here. Whether the Hebrew “thought, striving” words (רֵעַ, רְעוּת, רַעְיוֹן) and Daniel’s רַעְיוֹן also go back to ṣ́ “be pleased, desire”, or with ʿ to Arabic raʿā “be mindful of”, the evidence gathered does not settle; they stay here by spelling, with Arabic raʿā “be mindful of” as a possible cognate only. Brief tokens of רֵעַ include Mic 4:9 (“why do you cry aloud”, רֵעַ “shout”), which rua.json takes; Exo 32:17 likewise. Pro 18:24 לְהִתְרֹעֵעַ is רעע (“be broken”), playing on רֵעִים. Psa 2:9 תְּרֹעֵם is רעע “break”; the Greek’s ποιμανεῖς (Rev 2:27; 12:5; 19:15) reads it as רעה. רָעָה “evil” and רַע (root רעע) are not this root. Zero-token cross-reference keys m.dm.at, m.dm.au, t.br.ac, t.cm.ao, t.dh.ae, t.dk.ab, t.dk.ad, t.dm.aa, xt.al.aa are left out. Names of the root: רְעוּאֵל (names/reuel.json); רוּת Ruth (t.dl.ah), רְעוּ Reu (t.dl.ai) and רֵעִי Rei (t.dl.ak) have no name entries yet. The Greek-loans section of the brief offers διαλογισμός from רַעְיוֹן; that is Thayer saying the Septuagint uses it for the Aramaic word, not a loan, and it is entered only as a rendering. Peshitta words (SEDRA root 1774 ܪܥܐ: lexemes 3044 ܡܪܥܝܬܐ, 3045 ܪܥܐ, 3046 ܪܥܝܐ, 3047 ܪܥܝܐ; root 1777 ܪܥܐ: 3051 ܪܥܐ, 3052 ܪܥܝܢܐ, 3053 ܬܪܥܝܬܐ) were found by the database’s Peshitta tagging; their verses were not read in Syriac beyond the tagging. Not consulted: Payne Smith (Syriac senses), DULAT for Ugaritic rʿy “shepherd” (Segert’s glossary has only “friend”), Ge’ez rəʿya “pasture” (Dillmann, Leslau), CAD. Segert p. 201 and Biella p. 491 read from the scans’ text layers only. Open questions for review: (1) whether רְעוּת רוּחַ is “striving after wind” or “feeding on wind” (Hos 12:2), and whether the thought words belong under רצה; (2) Psa 37:3 “feed on faithfulness” or “befriend faithfulness”; (3) the reading of Ezk 34:23 and 37:24 in the first doctrine item as the kingdom at Christ’s return.
